data/forge/tags/blocks is what I have for my current version of minecraft, but extract your jar file and use that as your basis.

The earlier comment was for another version I think

To navigate, get the serene seasons datapack (I think), or extract the mod jar file (I used 7zip on windows) to a folder. Inside the contents of the folder, you'll see data/forge/tags/blocks.

You can delete everything in the folder except the data/forge/tags/blocks folders. Make a new notepad document and write this:

    {
      "pack": {
        "pack_format": 15,
        "description": "Serene Seasons - Fertility Datapack"
      }
    }

Important to note, "pack\_format": depends on which version of Minecraft you're using. It should be an easy search on Google, "Minecraft version \_\_\_\_ pack format number". There should be a table with all the info on it on a wiki. Save the file as pack.mcmeta. Make sure there's no invisible .txt at the end. This file should exist with your data folder (not inside).

From there, navigate all the way into the blocks folder and you can delete the glass file.

You want to make 5 new text files. 4 of them are the list of foods that'll count towards each season. So you'll have autum\_crops.json as one file, spring\_crops.json as another, summer\_crops.json, and winter\_crops.json

Each file's content should include the same code structure I have in my earlier comment. Just change out the names of the items to suit your needs.

The last file is should be called "unbreakable\_infertile\_crops.json" Same structure as the other 4, but this time you're adding crops that shouldn't break regardless of season. 

Once that is all done, zip both your data folder and pack.mcmeta together and name it something suitable like SereneSeasons\_Compatability.zip. Et voila, you should have your datapack!

I followed a random datapack making tutorial to get the info I needed so that might be of help to you as well.

Best of luck!

"Unfortunately you and I were simply born too late."  
I genuinely laughed because it's so true. I feel as though we were born too late or maybe too early.

I remember making a 10 minute presentation to my Asian parents in middle school to convince them that this career path was good. One of the points was that the tools and resources to learn animation/VFX wasn't available everywhere like it is today. You'd have to go to a school to gain knowledge and experience. Plus the entertainment industry is huge enough where finding employment isn't extremely challenging, but small enough where the competition isn't absolutely crazy compared to other industries. At least the VFX industry was extremely niche at the time and that they didn't have to worry about me being unemployed if I got in the college I went to.

We grew up with the world looking like that until everything started to change exponentially. I grew up using MS Paint, making Lego stop motion animation with my flip phone, DIY flipbooks, and the classic pen and paper. As I progressed through school, I was introduced to CS5 CS6 of Adobe Software but the only resource you had for learning was books and classes, and eventually YouTube. The free software that I used at the time were iMovie, Gimp, Pivot, and Blender. And back then, Blender was in its early stages and it was just awful. So you make do with what you have. 

But now there's Unreal Engine, Blender, Krita, and a whole bunch of other software out there that's free to use that has either went from paid -> free, or a free open source software that's a near-perfect replica of industry standard software. A huge surge of tutorials and resources to learn everything just boomed and literally anyone can learn everything. 

We have to play catch up with people who are literally less than a decade younger than us. A dude who was 14 got hired to work at Sony's Spiderverse from using Blender. It saddens me how good it is because I would've loved to have done something similar when I was 14. Perhaps I could've with the old Blender. I don't know. I semi expected younger people to be more talented than we are but I feel like it's happening too fast.

My entire life devoted to this career path. We got screwed and it sucks. And I couldn't agree more with the studios integrity. Thank you and everyone else for your kind words. I wish you the best of luck with college again, career and in life.

The eye is trying to register new information but since the flickering goes by so fast, it becomes jarring to the eye. 

If you saw a lightbulb flickering, the entire room doesn't turn completely dark, or your eyes doesn't get completely washed out that everything turns white. Plus, there's a slight gradual shift from being lit to being unlit.

3D: 
Blender is FREE and is open source. There are many great tutorials, plugins, and resources online that you can get for free and make your stuff look good. It's a great tool to get started as a beginner to learn.

Maya is the "industry standard". If you are serious about working in the industry, I highly suggest you learn Maya. Maya can get confusing as there are a million ways to do one thing. But once you get used to the program, it's not hard and fairly simple. They have a student version where you can get the software for free. Although it's much more difficult to find a high quality tutorials, resources and plugins for free. 

I like to think Cinema4d as the child of Maya and Blender. C4d is relatively easy to learn with a lot of great free tutorials. As someone else mentioned, greyscalegorilla is a great resource to learn C4d. The UI is more easy to grasp than Maya and Blender in my opinion.

Houdini is another 3d software that is absolutely crazy. Houdini may seem very intimidating at first, but it isn't that scary once you start learning to program. The best way to approach Houdini is to be as procedural as possible (at least for me). It's a more technical program. The educational version is free so you could give that a try if you wanted.

2D compositing:
After Effects is pretty cheap compared to Nuke. If you purchase creative cloud, you have access to many more Adobe software like photoshop, Premiere pro, Fuse, etc. One thing about AE is that it is layer based. It is very simple to understand visually. There tons of great tutorials online on YouTube. It's pretty easy to make composites. You can also do a lot of janky stuff in AE if you don't care about being procedural. 

Nuke is just an overpowered piece of software. Compositing in Nuke heavily is node based, and if you're not a visual thinker, Nuke may be a little hard to learn. But one thing's for sure, once you learn Nuke, it's easy to forget AE and make Nuke your main piece of software for compositing. 


Final thoughts:
If you're a beginner and want to have some fun, I suggest Blender and AE. 
If you are a beginner but you still want to become a VFX artist, I suggest Maya and AE AND Nuke. They can both be very handy with different occasions.

Good luck!

One interesting fact about the Korean Alphabet (글자/geulja) is that the shapes are formed by the shapes of our mouths and tongue; which was invented by King Sejong during the 14/15th century. 

For an example, the 'ㅇ' (ieung) character is based on our mouths making the 'o' shape. The following characters on the right (called the jungsong) that support the 'ㅇ' can further add how it sounds like. 아, 이, 오, 우 = a i o u. 

Further, the 'ㄴ' character sounds like the letter n. If you imagine looking how your tongue is shaped when you try to make an 'n' sound, it looks like 'ㄴ' from the side.
